summary: Jesse Hu frames AI agents as digital robots, transferring hard-won lessons from self-driving to agentic coding. The core thesis is a 1%-99% problem: the model is only a small fraction of the real-world system; the bulk is embodiment (tools, APIs, terminals, browsers, VMs), the offline stack (simulation, retraining, monitoring, human feedback), and deployment infrastructure. In self-driving, the winning team often had the best offline stack, not just the best model—a pattern he sees repeating in agents. He explores open-loop vs. closed-loop execution, noting that agents often run commands without observing outputs in real time, and highlights implicit design decisions such as time discretization: agents take conversational turns rather than continuously sampling the world at high frequency like robots do. He discusses input and action space design, citing Terminal Bench's Terminus agent and the Dreamer paper as examples of richer action spaces. He then addresses the shift from stateless to stateful agents: real agents must account for persistent VMs, file stores, Slack messages, and broader world state, complicating execution and evaluation. On the modeling side, he covers the DAgger/imitation-learning problem: agents trained on human demonstrations go out-of-distribution quickly, causing cascading failures. Self-driving from 2017–2020 over-focused on perception, assuming planning was easy; it took 8–10 years to learn that action models were the hard part—the same pattern now emerging with LLM agents. Hu also highlights why self-driving and coding agents are lucky: they benefit from predefined human interfaces with built-in telemetry, unlike broader knowledge-work tasks. He describes the hill-climbing process for iterating on complex systems, where simulation deploys with confidence and real-world logs feed back into simulation, grounding it. Categorized failure triage yields more insight than aggregate benchmark scores. He introduces the term agentics for the emerging discipline of agent development, noting that robotics concepts (MDPs, DAgger, offline RL, open/closed-loop control) transfer naturally because the problems are obvious in agent space. He closes by noting agents are only partway to reliable end-to-end work completion, with great demos and predictive models but not yet robust execution.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Jesse Hu introduces himself as a lifelong ML engineer with experience at YouTube (two-tower embeddings, BERT, mixture of experts), Waymo (ML/robotics, data, reward modeling, evaluation), and now Abundant (datasets and training for agentic coding models). He clarifies no Waymo inside information will be shared.

sections.title: The 1% vs. 99% Problem and Stack Parallels
sections.summary: Hu explains that the model is only 1% of real-world work; 99% is hardware, sensors, actuators, integration, deployment, and the offline stack (simulation, training, monitoring, human feedback). In agents, embodiment includes APIs, MCPs, terminals, browsers, VMs, and persistent file systems. The winning self-driving teams had the best offline stacks, enabling faster and more reliable development.

sections.title: Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop and Time Discretization
sections.summary: Robotics requires closing the loop—measuring real-world action outcomes to recalibrate. Agents often run open-loop (e.g., bash commands without real-time output observation). Agents also implicitly discretize time via conversational turns rather than continuous high-frequency sampling, which simplifies reasoning but prevents real-time interaction with pop-ups or long-running processes.

sections.title: Input and Action Space Design
sections.summary: Robotics offers explicit choices for input modalities (vision, LiDAR, radar) and action spaces (XY, continuous, 2D/3D, velocity, acceleration). Agents also have action space choices beyond MCPs and tool calls, such as character-level terminal interaction (Terminus agent) or frame-rate mouse/keyboard interaction (Dreamer paper). These implicit design decisions enable or limit agent capabilities.

sections.title: From Stateless to Stateful Agents
sections.summary: Unlike video-game driving where you spawn from nothing, real-world driving and real agents must account for persistent state. Agents are moving from stateless sessions to stateful VMs with persistent file stores, live Slack messages, and broader world state. This shift complicates both online execution and evaluation/simulation.

sections.title: DAgger, Imitation Learning, and Cascading Failures
sections.summary: Imitation learning (SFT from human demonstrations) causes agents to go rapidly out-of-distribution when encountering unseen states, such as browser pop-ups not present in training data. This cascading failure problem is well-studied in robotics (DAgger). The key theme: actions have consequences, and agents must predict, act, observe, and re-evaluate in a messy real world.

sections.title: Simulation, MDPs, and Action Models
sections.summary: Simulation represents real-world complexity and enables counterfactual rollout across all possible paths. MDPs provide a formalism for the agent-environment loop. Self-driving from 2017–2020 over-focused on perception, assuming planning was easy; it took 8–10 years to learn that action models were the hard part. The same pattern is emerging with LLM agents: sophisticated reasoning traces fail in real-world execution, proving that predictive models are not action models.

sections.title: Predefined Interfaces and Domain Luck
sections.summary: Hu explains why self-driving and coding agents are lucky domains: they have predefined human interfaces with built-in telemetry and electronic controls, making it easy to take actions and collect data. Broader knowledge-work tasks requiring full desktops are harder to codify. When exploring new domains, the presence of a predefined interface is a key consideration.

sections.title: Hill Climbing, Simulation, and Log Grounding
sections.summary: Hill climbing is the iterative guessing-and-checking process of improving complex systems against a benchmark. Self-driving uses simulation to deploy with confidence and learn, then feeds real-world logs back into simulation to ground it. Categorized failure triage—by city, error type, etc.—yields far more insight than aggregate benchmark scores. This offline tooling and process is central to Abundant's work.

sections.title: Current State, Agentics, and Closing
sections.summary: Hu notes agents are only partway to reliable end-to-end work completion, comparing today's agent state to early self-driving: great demos and predictive models but not robust execution. He recaps parallels: closed-loop systems, time discretization, action/input spaces, statefulness, predictive-to-action-model shift, simulation, and infrastructure. He introduces 'agentics' as the emerging discipline and recommends studying robotics literature (MDPs, DAgger, offline RL, open/closed-loop control) since problems are obvious in agent space. He shares his email for feedback.
